en: The Questions of King Milinda:
The Chapter on Similes, Section on Ants.
7. The Question on the Deer’s Limbs “Venerable Nāgasena, as for what you said—that ‘three limbs of a deer should be adopted’—which are those three limbs that should be adopted?
“Just as, Great King, a deer wanders in the forest by day and in the open air at night;”
In the same way, Great King, a practitioner engaged in yoga should dwell in the forest by day and in the open air at night.
This, Great King, is the first quality of the deer that should be adopted.
And this, Great King, was spoken by the Blessed One, the God beyond Gods, in the "Hair-Raising" discourse:
“Thus, Sāriputta, during those cold winter nights—the intervals between the eighth days when snow falls—I would dwell in the open air at night and in the forest grove by day.
During the last month of summer, I would dwell in the open air by day and in the forest grove at night.
Furthermore, Great King, when arrows or spears fall upon it, a deer dodges and flees; it does not present its body.
In the same way, Great King, when the defilements fall upon him, the practitioner of yoga must deceive them and flee; he must not allow his mind to be drawn toward them.
This, Great King, is the second quality of the deer that should be adopted.
Furthermore, Great King, when a deer sees people, it flees in this direction or that, thinking, "May they not see me."

In the same way, great king, when a practitioner of yoga sees those who are prone to quarreling, strife, contention, and dispute, who are immoral, indolent, and delight in company, he should flee by this way or that, thinking: "May they not see me, and may I not see them.
This, great king, is the third quality of the deer that should be adopted.
This was also said, Great King, by the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma:
“May I never have an evil wish,
nor be indolent or of inferior energy.”
“Though he was of little learning and improper conduct,
he was once highly esteemed somewhere.
Thus ends the seventh inquiry, the Question of Miggaṅga.
